name: Model Liability and Errors and Omissions
blurb: Cover for what a model does. Algorithmic bias class actions in hiring, lending and tenant screening, autonomous agents executing bad transactions, diagnostic AI malpractice, hallucinated professional advice, autonomous vehicle product liability, trading bot losses, industrial control misconfiguration, chatbot defamation and unauthorised commitments, coding assistant vulnerabilities, and deepfake wire fraud.

reading.body:
Model liability is being split into ten distinct cover categories, from hiring bias to industrial control errors, which means AI risk is priced by what the output does in a specific domain rather than as one technology exposure.

The ten categories divide into claims about what a model says and claims about what it does. On the speech side sit algorithmic bias in hiring, mortgage processing, tenant screening and healthcare, hallucinated professional advice, and chatbot defamation or unauthorised commitments. On the action side sit autonomous agent execution failures, diagnostic AI that misses a critical condition, autonomous vehicle collisions, trading bot loops, improper adjustments by process control AI in plants and refineries, security flaws introduced by generated code, and deepfake-induced wire transfers. The action side is where the exposure leaves the screen and reaches a patient, a road, a trading book or a refinery.

Liability here attaches to the domain rather than to the model. A diagnostic tool that misses a condition is malpractice, a process control model that adjusts a plant improperly is an industrial claim, and a coding assistant that ships a vulnerability is a software claim. That means the deployment decision sets the exposure, and the same underlying capability carries different cover depending on where it is pointed. The diagnostic category also names both health systems and developers, so the exposure is not confined to whoever trained the model.

What the data does not contain is any measure of how often these claims occur or what they cost. Ten is a count of exposure types, not of incidents, and there are no premiums, payouts, jurisdictions or judgments attached to any of them. Nothing in this taxonomy connects to compute, data centers or power, so it cannot speak to whether AI scaling is constrained by the grid. It describes how the legal and insurance surface around model outputs is being carved up, and stops there.
